newsitem.title: CHINA: North Korea in downward spiral after floods.
newsitem.headline: North Korea in downward spiral after floods.

text.p: Malnourished children with protruding bellies and stick-like arms can be seen in North Korea, and many of the nation's 22 million people could die if food shortages worsen next year, a U.N. official said on Friday.

Savage floods have destroyed 10 percent of North Korea's grain harvest this year, aggravating food shortages in the already hungry nation, Robert Hauser, former country director of the United Nations World Food Programme in North Korea, told a news conference in Beijing.
"The country is definitely in a downward spiral," said Hauser, who finished his assignment this month.
"If you go out into the countryside you see skinny people only," he said. Many children had pot bellies, stick-like arms, visible ribs and skin rashes -- clear symptoms of malnutrition.
"This year they may just make it...but next year the crisis will be worse," Hauser said.
"Disasters will happen more easily...and will happen more frequently," he said, attributing the growing danger to erosion and deforestation, with much wood bartered for precious food.
Food shortages in the coming winter months coupled with the need for farmers to do an enormous amount of physical and manual work in the fields threatened rural residents.

"They will be completely exhausted when they hit the hunger period," Hauser said. "When the disaster happens...it will be a disaster of 22 million people...the population as a whole coming to the crunch."
"They will die anywhere and everywhere in the country," he said.

North Korea was still reeling from devastating floods last year -- the worst to ravage the country in a century -- when torrential rains struck in July, triggering new flooding across its southern grain basket.
About 373,000 tonnes of grain were lost, or one-tenth of the year's output, Hauser said.
The government and people appeared to be working together to escape the spiral toward famine, Hauser said.
Pyongyang could not increase the area under grain because land was not available, he said, adding that it also could not boost the yield due to shortages of fertilisers and pesticides.
It was seeking foreign investment and technology, but faced stagnation throughout its industry, agriculture and commerce, he said.
The floods have inundated several coal mines, including one of the largest in North Korea, he said.
However, few North Koreans had tried to flee because of checkpoints across the country and government rationing of food by issuing coupons limited to local districts, he said.
Hauser painted a gloomy picture ahead, despite Pyongyang's efforts to ease the shortages.
"It is 22 million people who have less and less, and less and less to eat," Hauser said.
North Koreans have been rationed to 200 gm (seven oz) of cereals per person per day or six kg (13.2 lb) per person per month since last year.

Despite its philosophy of self-reliance, Pyongyang asked for help last year from the international community. But its pleas have largely been ignored due to opposition from the U.S. and South Korean governments.
The World Food Programme hoped to give North Korea 70,550 tonnes of cereals and blended foods worth $25.9 million.
About 38,000 tonnes worth $15.6 million have been pledged and were under delivery, or 60 percent of the target.
